body.objective: Students will be able to choose parts for an arrangement.
body.iCan: I can choose parts for an arrangement.
successCriteria: I can identify the layers of a song
I can assign melody, harmony, bass and rhythm to available instruments
I can write a simple lead sheet or part chart
body.hook: When a song moves from a full studio band to a high school ensemble of three guitars, a ukulele and a cajón, someone has to decide who plays what. That person is the arranger, and good arrangements make small groups sound full.

study.title: Who Plays What?
study.question: How do arrangers adapt a song for the musicians they have?
study.passage:
Step 1, Listen for layers (10 minutes): Listen to a simple song (teacher's choice, for example a folk song or a pop ballad). List every layer: melody (voice), countermelody, chords (pads or guitar), bass, drums or percussion, effects.
Step 2, Inventory (5 minutes): List the instruments and voices in your group and their ranges and strengths.
Step 3, Assign (15 minutes): Every arrangement needs four jobs: melody (clear and on top), harmony (chords), bass (low root notes) and rhythm (pulse). Assign each job. If you have extra players, add a countermelody or double the melody at the octave. Check ranges: is the melody too high for the singer? Transpose if needed.
Step 4, Part chart (15 minutes): Make a chart with each section of the song (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro) across the top and each player down the side. Write what each plays: "chords, strum pattern 1," "bass on roots, half notes," "rest." Plan contrast: thin in verses, full in choruses.
Step 5, Rehearse (10 minutes): Run the arrangement once and adjust.

examples.title: Four jobs
examples.problem: A group has voice, guitar, keyboard and cajón. Assign the four jobs.
examples.answer: Voice melody, guitar chords, keyboard left-hand bass, cajón rhythm
examples.explore: What could the keyboard right hand add?

examples.title: Range
examples.problem: The melody goes too high for the singer. What can you do?
examples.answer: Move the song down to a lower key

examples.title: Contrast
examples.problem: How can a chorus feel bigger than a verse?
examples.answer: Bring in drums and countermelody; strum full chords
examples.explore: What could drop out in the bridge?

examples.title: Bass line
examples.problem: Write a bass line for C-G-Am-F.
examples.answer: C, G, A, F in half or whole notes
examples.explore: How could passing notes connect them?

practice.q: How would you arrange a song with no bass instrument?
